passage:
“Chinmay, your phone's buzzing again.”
“I know, Tanuja.” He turned it face down on the canteen table.
“Is it the batch group? Oh, the voice-note thing.” She laughed, then stopped. “Come on, it's only ragging. Everyone gets a nickname in first year.”
“They've posted my voice note forty times. With a goat sound over it.”
“That's just their humour. Don't take it so seriously.”
“Tanuja, I haven't spoken in class for two weeks. I rehearse every answer in my head and then I stay quiet, because someone might record it.”
She put her spoon down.
“I keep hearing 'it's fun',” he said. “But nobody laughing is the one who can't sleep. It's not fun. They're mocking me every night and I hate it.”
Tanuja looked at his phone, then at him. “Okay. Then I won't call it fun again. Show me the messages.”

qa.q: How many times has Chinmay's voice note been posted in the group?
qa.a: His voice note has been posted forty times, with a goat sound over it.

qa.q: Why does Chinmay insist on saying plainly what the messages are?
qa.a: He feels hurt and dismissed, because the word 'fun' hides that he has gone silent in class and can't sleep; naming it as mocking makes his distress real.

qa.q: What could Tanuja do after reading the messages?
qa.a: She could stay with Chinmay, help him save the messages, and go with him to the anti-ragging cell or a warden instead of calling it humour.

qa.q: How does Tanuja's view change during the conversation?
qa.a: At first she sees ordinary first-year teasing; once Chinmay describes staying silent and sleepless, she sees real harm and stops using the word fun.

grounding: The passage shows a student whose distress is brushed off as ragging or fun until he names the mocking plainly.

passage:
Looking back, the worst part was not the stickers. It was the word everyone used for them.
In my second semester, the hostel group started pasting my face onto cartoon rats. Every morning there would be a new one. I, Rafiq, became “Ratfiq” to thirty people.
When I told Vasudha, my lab partner, she shrugged. “It's banter. They do it to everyone they like.” I nodded, because nodding was easier. For weeks I told myself the same thing: banter, harmless, a sign of being liked.
But I was eating dinner in my room to avoid the mess. I had muted the group and still checked it at 2 a.m.
One evening I wrote the true sentence in my notes app: they are humiliating me and I dread every morning. Seeing it written down, I finally went to the student counsellor, and I stopped calling it banter.

qa.q: What did the hostel group paste the narrator's face onto?
qa.a: They pasted Rafiq's face onto cartoon rats, and a new one appeared every morning.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq keep repeating the word banter for weeks?
qa.a: Rafiq felt ashamed and wanted to fit in, so the friendly word was a comfort; admitting humiliation felt harder than nodding along.

qa.q: What helped Rafiq move from confusion to action?
qa.a: Writing one plain, true sentence about the humiliation and dread; it made the harm clear enough to take to the student counsellor.

qa.q: How might Vasudha see the stickers differently if she had known about the dinners in the room and the 2 a.m. checking?
qa.a: She might stop calling it banter and see that Rafiq was hurting and needed support, not a shrug.

grounding: The passage shows repeated group-chat mockery being relabelled as banter, and the receiver finally naming the distress plainly.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Thursday.
Sahil (first-year, B.Com) came in at 11 a.m. and sat without speaking for almost a minute. He had screenshots ready on his phone. In the section group, several classmates post edited photos of him with captions about his weight, most nights for the past month.
He said he had raised it with Yogesh, the class representative, who told him it was "just ragging, a tradition, nothing personal." Sahil repeated that phrase twice, as if checking whether he was allowed to be upset.
I told him plainly that what he described is repeated mocking, that his distress makes sense, and that it is not his fault.
Next steps: with his consent I forwarded the screenshots to the anti-ragging committee the same afternoon, and the convenor called him before 5 p.m. I have asked to meet Yogesh tomorrow about how complaints are handled. Follow-up with Sahil on Monday.

qa.q: Who told Sahil it was just ragging?
qa.a: Yogesh, the class representative, told him it was “just ragging, a tradition, nothing personal.”

qa.q: Why did Sahil repeat Yogesh's phrase twice?
qa.a: He seemed unsure and ashamed, as if checking whether he was allowed to feel hurt when the mocking had been called a tradition.

qa.q: Which of the counsellor's steps helped most, and what could come next?
qa.a: The counsellor named the behaviour as repeated mocking, told Sahil it was not his fault and passed the screenshots to the committee the same day; next, the meeting with Yogesh can change how complaints are handled.

qa.q: How might Yogesh's words have felt to Sahil?
qa.a: They made Sahil's pain sound silly and unimportant, so he was left feeling unheard and doubting his own reaction.

grounding: The note shows a student's distress over group-chat mocking being dismissed as ragging, and an adult naming it plainly.

passage:
Tuesday, late.
The town hall was forty minutes long and nobody said the word people. Mridul, our department head, said “rightsizing” eleven times. I counted. “Optimising the support layer.” “Aligning capacity.”
Everyone clapped at the end. I clapped too, then felt a bit sick about it.
At the question slot I put my hand up. My voice shook. I asked, “Which teams, and what happens to them? Do the support staff in Nagpur lose their jobs, and when?”
It went very quiet. Mridul paused, then said, “Around sixty roles in Nagpur, over three months.”
Sixty roles. Sixty people, many of whom I've trained on video calls. Madhavi with the twins. The new joiner who asked me how to set up his leave.
Afterward, two colleagues messaged me: “thank you for asking that.” I'm still shaky. But now we are talking about people, not a layer. — Yogesh

qa.q: How many times did Mridul say “rightsizing”?
qa.a: Mridul said “rightsizing” eleven times during the town hall.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel after clapping at the end of the town hall?
qa.a: Yogesh felt uneasy and a bit sick, because the soft words had hidden what was happening to real colleagues.

qa.q: Which question made the difference, and why did it work?
qa.a: Asking which teams and what happens to them; the plain question forced an answer in people and months instead of labels.

qa.q: What is it like for the two colleagues who messaged Yogesh?
qa.a: They seem relieved and grateful that someone asked out loud what they may have been afraid to ask themselves.

grounding: The diary shows an employee meeting the label rightsizing by asking what actually happens to whom, which brings attention back to people.

passage:
The milk society office in Kuttikkad smelled of wet cans and diesel. Jomon, the new supervisor, tapped the notice on the board. “We are just restructuring the collection route. More efficient.”
Pallavi, who kept the accounts, read it twice. The Pullur point was simply missing.
“Jomon chetta, restructuring means what, exactly? Who stops being collected?”
He waved a hand. “Only the far hamlet. Four or five suppliers.”
“It's six,” she said, turning the ledger toward him. “Sarojini amma, Thankamma, the two brothers with the buffalo, and old Varghese. They'd have to carry their cans three kilometres to the main road, before six in the morning.”
Jomon looked at the names for a long moment. Outside, the collection van coughed and started.
“I didn't think of it as people,” he said quietly. “Let's put it in the committee meeting on Friday. Write down those names for me.”

qa.q: How many suppliers at the Pullur point does Pallavi count in the ledger?
qa.a: She counts six suppliers, including Sarojini amma, Thankamma, the two brothers and old Varghese.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel when he looked at the names for a long moment?
qa.a: He seemed uncomfortable and a little ashamed, realising the word restructuring had hidden real people from him.

qa.q: What approach worked for Pallavi, and why?
qa.a: She turned the ledger toward him and read out names and distances; concrete people and consequences are harder to wave away than a label.

qa.q: What would it be like for Sarojini amma if the route change went ahead unexamined?
qa.a: She would have to carry heavy cans three kilometres to the road before dawn, with no one having asked her.

grounding: The passage shows an adult asking what a restructuring label actually means for whom, and plain words turning attention back to the people affected.

“And if you had said yes?”

Friday: Madhuri's tiffin fell and her rice spilled on the steps. Nobody moved. Keerthana stood with the rope in her hand and thought, If everyone waits for everyone, nobody ever helps. Her stomach felt tight. She walked over, picked up the tiffin lid and said, “You can take my end of the rope.”

qa.a: Being one of eight made her feel less responsible, and she was probably afraid of standing out from the group.

Vidya, come sit. You said Tanvir is being left out and it isn't your doing. Let me, your Nana Wasim, tell you something.
When I was ten, in Mhow, there was a boy called Shafiq who stammered. The rest of us decided he couldn't play gilli-danda with us. I didn't decide it, you see. Iqbal decided it. I just stood with Iqbal.

Noa had taken it for a laugh. That evening Liv messaged, “Send it to the class chat, it's hilarious,” and Noa did.

“Liv told me to,” Noa said quickly. “It was her idea. I just sent it.”

Subject: About the photo

Shreya,

I know you're angry and you have every right. I want to explain what happened with the photo from the sports day changing room.

I didn't plan it. Kiran was the one who said, “Send it to the gang, she'll laugh too.” Everyone in the group was waiting. If I hadn't sent it, someone else would have. Honestly, I was the messenger.

I saw the clip at 11 p.m., in the college meme page. Nandini tripping on the stage steps at the fest, slowed down, with a sad trombone and a caption about her walk.
The comments grew as I watched. Laughing faces. Someone guessed her roll number. Someone wrote her surname wrong on purpose.

I still remember the exact sentence Thomas used: “Just move batch 14 to dispatch. Don't log the seal failures.”
We make pressure-cooker gaskets. Batch 14 had eleven samples that leaked under test. Thomas was my manager and he was under pressure; the order was already late.
I said, “I understand what you're asking, and I understand why.” Then I said the part that made my voice go thin: “But if one of these fails in someone's kitchen, it's me who signed the test sheet. I can't hand my name over to you.”
He was angry. I went back to my desk shaking and wrote a short, factual email to the quality head, attaching the test data.
She called me within the hour, put batch 14 on hold that afternoon and told Thomas herself.
I'm Naveen; I've been on the line four years. I lost sleep that week. I don't regret it.

I was at the inspection bench this morning when Darshan, the line manager, told Payal to "keep the hairline cracks off the report — they're cosmetic, the client won't notice." The parts were brake-lever brackets.

Payal's hands were unsteady afterward. I told her she had done her job well.

Wed, 11:30 p.m.
Keerthana came to my desk at 6 today, bag already on her shoulder. “The spindle sensors that failed calibration, just release them. I'll take responsibility.”
I said okay. I actually said okay. Then I sat there after she left and felt the word sit in my stomach.
Because it's my login on the release screen. It's my name the auditors will see. She can take responsibility for telling me. She can't take it for my click.
So at 8 I emailed her: “I understand the instruction. I can't release lot 7B without logging the failed calibration. I'm copying the quality lead so we decide properly.”
The quality lead replied at 9:40: “Thanks for flagging. Lot on hold. Let's all meet at 10 tomorrow.”
Keerthana hasn't replied. I'm nervous about tomorrow. But I'd rather be nervous than be the person who clicked. — Ritu

qa.a: She asked Ritu to release the spindle sensors that failed calibration, lot 7B.

qa.a: Ritu felt uneasy because the login and the name on the release screen were Ritu's own, so Keerthana's promise to take responsibility couldn't really cover Ritu's click.

passage:
Monday: Kunal and his brother came from Gali No. 4 with a cricket ball. Baljeet folded his arms. “Not with them. They're dirty. They live like jungli animals over there.” The others laughed, and Kunal left.
Wednesday: The Gali No. 4 kids' ball rolled into Baljeet's lane. Baljeet kicked it into the drain. “They're wild anyway, they won't care.” Nobody stopped him. It felt easy, almost funny.
Saturday: The lane flooded after rain. Baljeet's little sister Simran slipped near the drain and her chappal floated off. It was Kunal who waded in, fished it out and gave it back, then quietly wiped her knee with his sleeve.
Baljeet stood very still. Kunal's hands were muddy, just like his own. He did not look wild at all. Baljeet mumbled, “Thanks,” and couldn't meet his eyes.

qa.q: Where did Baljeet kick the ball on Wednesday?
qa.a: He kicked the Gali No. 4 kids' ball into the drain.

qa.q: Why did kicking the ball feel easy to Baljeet on Wednesday?
qa.a: Calling the children wild made him feel their feelings didn't count, so being rough felt almost funny instead of mean.

qa.q: What could Baljeet do next time he sees Kunal?
qa.a: He could invite Kunal to play cricket and say sorry about the ball, getting to know him as a person rather than as “Gali No. 4”.

qa.q: How might Kunal see Baljeet's lane after Monday and Wednesday?
qa.a: Kunal probably felt insulted and unwelcome there, yet he still helped Simran, which shows he did not answer cruelty with cruelty.

grounding: The beats show a child calling children from another lane dirty and wild, which makes rough treatment feel acceptable until he sees one of them as a person.

passage:
Sahil, you called those boys from the railway quarters “rats” at dinner. Let me, your Karthik mama, tell you where that word took me once.
When I was nine, in Kollam, we lived near the fishermen's colony. We called their children “smelly crabs.” We wouldn't let them near our temple ground to play. One day my friends threw sand in a small boy's eyes and I laughed. Crabs, after all. Who cares what a crab feels?
That boy was Sebastian. Years later, in college, he was the one who stayed up all night with me when my father was in hospital. He never mentioned the sand. I did, finally, and cried saying sorry.
I had made him a crab so I didn't have to see him. Once I saw him, I couldn't unsee it.

qa.q: What did the children call the boys from the fishermen's colony?
qa.a: They called them “smelly crabs” and wouldn't let them play on the temple ground.

qa.q: Why did young Karthik laugh when sand was thrown in the boy's eyes?
qa.a: Calling the boy a crab made his pain seem unreal, so Karthik felt no guilt at the time and laughing felt harmless.

qa.q: At what moment in the story could young Karthik have chosen differently?
qa.a: When his friends threw sand, he could have stopped laughing, helped the boy and refused to use the word crabs again.

qa.q: How might Sebastian have felt about the sand when Karthik finally apologised?
qa.a: Sebastian had likely been hurt long ago but may have felt respected and understood when Karthik named it and said sorry.

grounding: The uncle's memory shows children labelling another group as animals, which made rough treatment feel acceptable.

The power had gone at five, and the whole society poured downstairs to escape the heat. There was only one lit patch, under the generator lamp near Tower B.
Baljeet and the other kids from Tower D came with a tennis ball.
Ojas stood in the middle of the lit patch. “No D-wing kids. You lot are wild, you break everything, you're like monkeys.” His friends nodded.
Baljeet said, “There's no other light.”
“Not our problem,” Ojas said, and bounced the ball hard off Baljeet's shoulder. It stung. The D-wing kids went and sat in the dark near the gate.
Ojas's mother had seen the ball hit. She came over and said, calmly, “Would you bounce a ball off Baljeet's shoulder if you didn't call him a monkey first?”
Ojas started to answer, then couldn't. The word had made it feel allowed.

qa.q: Where was the only lit patch during the power cut?
qa.a: It was under the generator lamp near Tower B.

qa.q: Why did bouncing the ball off Baljeet's shoulder feel allowed to Ojas?
qa.a: Calling the D-wing kids wild monkeys made Ojas feel they didn't count as real children, so hurting them felt less wrong.

qa.q: Which part of the mother's response helped Ojas see it?
qa.a: She stayed calm and asked a question that connected the label to the hurt, letting Ojas see it for himself.

qa.q: What is it like for the D-wing kids to sit in the dark near the gate?
qa.a: They feel rejected and left out, stuck in the heat and the dark while being called monkeys by a neighbour.

grounding: The passage shows a child calling children from another building wild and refusing to share play space, which makes rough treatment feel acceptable.

The bus stand in Barwani was hot and slow. Vikas held court on the bench.
“The harvest-labour families are back,” he said, jerking his chin toward a truck unloading bundles by the ginning mill. “Goats with phones. You can smell them from here.”
Uday laughed, because the others did. Vikas told another one, about how they “breed like cattle.” More laughs.
A girl from the truck, maybe fourteen like them, was helping an old woman down the step. She dropped a steel tumbler; it rolled toward the bench. Vikas pushed it back with his foot without looking up.
Uday picked it up instead and held it out. The girl said, “Thank you, bhaiya,” in careful Hindi.
Vikas snorted. But Uday felt something shift. The joke only worked if you didn't look at her face. He stopped laughing for the rest of the afternoon.

qa.q: What did Vikas do when the steel tumbler rolled toward the bench?
qa.a: He pushed it back with his foot without looking up.

qa.q: Why did the jokes feel easy and funny to Vikas?
qa.a: Calling the families goats and cattle kept them faceless, so Vikas felt superior and didn't have to feel any empathy.

qa.q: What could Uday try the next time Vikas starts these jokes?
qa.a: He could stop laughing openly and say something simple, like mentioning the girl who thanked him, to put a face back on the group.

qa.q: How might the girl from the truck see the boys on the bench?
qa.a: She may feel unwelcome and wary of them, but Uday's small kindness might make her feel seen.

grounding: The passage shows a teenager repeating jokes that call an outsider group animals, making cruelty easy until someone looks at one face.

passage:
Every Friday, the lads from Fjell School crossed the bridge to use the Solberg pitch. And every Friday, Oskar had a new joke.
“Here come the hill trolls. Do they even speak, or just grunt?”
Xin smiled a little, not really amused. Oskar kept going: “They're like sheep. Follow the one with the ball.”
It got easier with every week. Oskar didn't know their names. He didn't want to.
This Friday, one of the Fjell boys went down hard on the concrete edge and didn't get up. Xin ran over. Oskar followed slowly.
The boy was holding his wrist, face white, trying not to cry in front of strangers. Xin knelt. “What's your name?”
“Emil.”
Oskar stood there. Emil. Not a troll, not a sheep. A fifteen-year-old whose hands were shaking. Oskar felt his face burn, then went to fetch the coach.

qa.q: What did Oskar call the boys from Fjell School?
qa.a: He called them “hill trolls” and said they were like sheep.

qa.q: Why did the jokes get easier for Oskar week after week?
qa.a: Not knowing their names let him feel superior and distant, so mocking them didn't make him uncomfortable.

qa.q: What did Xin do that worked?
qa.a: Xin ran to help and asked the boy's name, which turned “trolls” back into a real person called Emil.

qa.q: How might Emil see the Solberg pitch after this Friday?
qa.a: Emil might have felt scared and embarrassed after falling among strangers who mocked his school, but Xin's kindness could make him feel less alone.

grounding: The passage shows a teenager's jokes calling an outside group animals stripping them of faces, until one boy's name brings empathy back.

passage:
Hostel mess, St. Mary's, Wednesday dinner.
Seema was on a roll. “The sports-quota lot came in stinking again. Buffaloes. They eat like buffaloes, they think like buffaloes.” Her table laughed.
Shreya, who was sports-quota, was two seats down, peeling an orange very slowly.
“Not you, obviously,” Seema added, as if that fixed it.
Mrs D'Souza, the mess warden, stopped by their table. “Seema, who's your partner in the chemistry practical?”
“Tanu.”
“Tanu's sports-quota. Is she a buffalo?”
Seema's laugh faltered. “That's different, I know her.”
“Exactly,” said the warden, and walked on.
Seema looked at Shreya properly for the first time that evening. Shreya's ears were red. Seema didn't know what to say, so for once, she said nothing funny.

qa.q: What did Seema call the sports-quota students?
qa.a: She called them buffaloes and said they eat and think like buffaloes.

qa.q: Why did Seema add “Not you, obviously” to Shreya?
qa.a: She was a little uncomfortable seeing Shreya there, but still felt the group joke was harmless as long as it wasn't about someone she knew.

qa.q: What made the warden's question effective?
qa.a: Asking about one real person Seema knew showed her that the insult only held up when the group had no faces.

qa.q: What is it like for Shreya to sit two seats down during the jokes?
qa.a: Shreya feels hurt and embarrassed, and being told “not you” doesn't help, because the insult is still about her group.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager making jokes that strip an outside group of faces, and how knowing one person makes the cruelty harder.

passage:
The Pune hostel office had a queue down the stairs. When Ishita reached the counter, the clerk didn't look up.
“Roll?”
“Forty-seven. I'm Ishita Chanu, from Imphal. My mess card isn't...”
“Forty-seven, north-east quota. You people always have card problems.” He slid a form across. “Next.”
It was the third time that week. The accounts section called her “the Imphal case.” The PT sir called her “Chinky” once, then laughed like it was nothing.
She walked back holding the form, feeling strangely thin, as if she were fading around the edges.
At the gate, Jahnavi, her lab partner, waved hard. “Ishita! Where were you? We saved you a plate of poha. Come, sit.”
Ishita sat. Jahnavi talked about the practical, asked about her mother's cold, said her name three more times without noticing.
Ishita felt herself come back, slowly.

qa.q: What number did the clerk use for Ishita?
qa.a: The clerk used her roll number, forty-seven, and called her “north-east quota.”

qa.q: How did Ishita feel walking back from the office?
qa.a: She felt hurt and invisible, “strangely thin” as if fading, because she kept being treated as a number or a case.

qa.q: How could a friend support someone treated like this?
qa.a: Like Jahnavi, by using their name, saving them a place and asking about their life, and by helping them report the slur to the college.

qa.q: How does Jahnavi see Ishita compared with the office staff?
qa.a: Jahnavi sees a friend with a name and a mother with a cold, not a roll number or quota.

grounding: The passage shows a migrant student being treated as a number and a problem, and being steadied by a friend who addresses her by name.

“Uma? You've gone quiet.” Ganga, her cousin, sounded tinny on speaker.
“Sorry. Long day.”
“What happened?”
“Nothing. The landlord came to collect rent. He talked to my roommate the whole time. About me. ‘These Bihar students, always late, always a headache.’ I was standing right there.”
“Did he say your name?”
“He doesn't know it. I'm ‘the Bihar one’. At the bank today, same. The man said, ‘You people, go to the other counter.’”
“Uma.”
“I just feel like a burden everywhere, Ganga-di. Like a problem on legs.”
“Listen. You are Uma, who made the top score in our district. Who fixes Nani's phone every holiday. Say it.”
Uma half laughed, half cried. “I'm Uma.”
“Good. Now tell me about your college friends. Who knows your name there?”
“Farzana. And Joel.”
“Call them tomorrow. Eat with them. Stay with people who see you.”

qa.a: He called her “the Bihar one” and talked about “these Bihar students” as a headache.

qa.q: How does Uma feel after the landlord and the bank?
qa.a: She feels like a burden and invisible, “a problem on legs,” because nobody addresses her by name.

qa.q: What did Ganga advise, and why might it help?
qa.a: To spend time with Farzana and Joel, people who know her name; staying connected to people who see her helps her feel human again.

qa.q: If you were Ganga, hearing Uma go quiet, what would you want?
qa.a: Ganga would want Uma to feel remembered and not alone, which is why she reminds her of who she is.

grounding: The dialogue shows a migrant student treated as a burden and not addressed by name, and the comfort of staying connected to someone who sees her.

passage:
My first month in Delhi, I learned that I had several new names.
At the admissions desk I was “Nepal,” as in, “Nepal, sit there.” The flat owner wrote “Nepali girl” on the rent receipt instead of Binita Gurung. In the seminar, a professor once said, “Students like you cost the department,” and I spent the whole period staring at my notebook, feeling like a mistake.
I started going small. Eating late so the kitchen was empty. Not raising my hand.
It was Noor who noticed. She sat next to me in the library one evening and said, “Binita, you haven't told me one story about home. Tell me about Pokhara.” So I did. The lake, my father's tea stall, the dog that follows everyone.
We still meet every Thursday. When the world forgets my name, I know one person who never does.

qa.q: What did the flat owner write on the rent receipt?
qa.a: The flat owner wrote “Nepali girl” instead of Binita Gurung.

qa.q: How did Binita feel during the seminar comment, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and unwanted, staring at her notebook “feeling like a mistake” after being described as a cost.

qa.q: What helped Binita, and what could the college do too?
qa.a: Noor's regular, personal attention helped; the college could also make sure staff address students by name and take complaints about such remarks seriously.

qa.q: How does Noor see Binita?
qa.a: Noor sees her as a person with stories and a home in Pokhara, not as “Nepal” or a cost.

grounding: The first-person account shows a migrant student treated as a number or burden and the steadying effect of a friend who uses her name.

passage:
The café in Valencia was loud with the Saturday rush. Felix stirred his coffee hard.
“Those delivery riders are a plague. They all ride on the pavement. They're all the same, zero manners.”
Valentina nodded, then didn't. “All of them?”
“Every one.”
She glanced at the window. A rider in a green jacket was waiting by the pick-up shelf, rubbing his hands against the cold. She'd seen him before.
“That one,” she said. “Want to ask him something?” Before Felix could object, she held the door. “Hi, sorry. How many deliveries do you do on a Saturday?”
The rider blinked. “Thirty, if it goes well. My name's Joaquín. I'm saving for my engineering exams.” He smiled, tired. “Most people don't ask.”
When he left, Felix was quiet. “Okay. He's not a plague,” he admitted. “He's a guy who's cold.”

qa.q: How many deliveries does Joaquín do on a good Saturday?
qa.a: He does thirty deliveries on a Saturday if it goes well.

qa.q: Why did Valentina hesitate after first nodding?
qa.a: She felt uneasy with Felix's “all the same” contempt, because she had seen that rider before and knew he was one real person.

qa.q: What did Valentina do that worked?
qa.a: She turned a sweeping label into one conversation, asking the rider directly so Felix heard a name and a real story.

qa.q: How might Joaquín feel when a customer asks him a question?
qa.a: He might feel surprised and respected, since “most people don't ask,” and briefly less invisible.

grounding: The scene shows an adult responding to contempt for a group by talking to one person from it, which brings back empathy.

The staff room of the district hospital had one kettle and a lot of complaints.
“The night cleaners are useless,” Yusuf said, dropping into a chair. “Lazy lot. Ward 6 was filthy again.”
Lalremsiami poured her tea. “Which cleaner does Ward 6?”
Yusuf blinked. “I don't know. One of them.”
“It's Parvati,” she said. “She's alone for three wards since two of them left. She told me last week she's asked for a second trolley four times.”
“Alone? For three?”
“Alone. She's also the one who found the patient on the floor near the lift last month and called us.”
Yusuf sat quietly for a moment. “I thought there were six of them on nights.”
“There used to be.”
He put his cup down. “I'll write to the admin about the staffing. And I'll introduce myself to Parvati tonight.”

qa.a: Parvati covers three wards alone since two cleaners left.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling when he learned Parvati worked alone?
qa.a: He was surprised and a little ashamed, because the word lazy had hidden a real person doing the work of several.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami's question do well?
qa.a: Asking “which cleaner” moved Yusuf from a faceless “lazy lot” to one named person and her real situation.

qa.q: How might Parvati feel if Yusuf introduces himself tonight?
qa.a: She may feel respected and noticed after being overlooked, and hopeful that someone will finally support her request for help.

grounding: The scene shows an adult answering contempt for a group by naming one person in it, which brings back empathy and action.

passage:
Dear Farida,

I have been meaning to write since Sunday.

You may not know this, but a few weeks ago, at the parish meeting, I heard someone call the families in the resettlement colony “encroachers,” people who “only take.” I nodded. I didn't know any of you.

Then on Sunday you told us about your brother Imran, who works double shifts at the bus depot and still teaches the colony children maths every evening under the streetlight. You told us how your mother cried when the demolition notice came.

I kept picturing Imran with the chalk and the streetlight. I couldn't nod again.

At the next meeting, I plan to ask whoever speaks that way which family they actually mean, and to invite you to speak if you're willing.

Thank you for telling me a real story.

Warmly,
Francis

qa.q: Where does Farida's brother Imran work?
qa.a: Imran works double shifts at the bus depot.

qa.q: Why could Francis not nod again at contemptuous talk about the colony?
qa.a: After hearing about Imran and the streetlight, Francis felt moved and uncomfortable, because the families now had faces.

qa.q: What does Francis plan to do at the next meeting, and why might it help?
qa.a: Francis will ask which family the speaker actually means and invite Farida to speak; asking about one person breaks sweeping contempt.

qa.q: How might Farida feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Farida may feel heard and respected, and perhaps relieved that telling the story about Imran made a difference.

grounding: The letter shows an adult who once accepted contempt for a group changing after listening to one real story from someone in it.
